passages.happening:
When the land is divided, a portion is to be set apart for the LORD, ‘a holy portion of the land 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 cubits wide’ (verse 1), with the sanctuary in it and room for the priests and the Levites (verses 2-5). Beside it lie the city's portion and land for the prince on either side (verses 6-7). ‘This land will be his possession in Israel. And My princes will no longer oppress My people’ (verse 8).

“Enough, O princes of Israel! Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right. Stop dispossessing My people” (verse 9). ‘You must use honest scales, a just ephah, and a just bath’ (verse 10), and fixed standards for measures and weights (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
Ezekiel had watched Judah's kings abuse their power. Jehoiakim built a palace with forced labor, the prophets accused the ruling class of seizing fields and houses, and the story of Naboth shows how a king could take a family's inheritance by legal fraud. By giving the prince his own land, the vision removes the excuse for taking other people's.

The ruler is called the prince, not the king. He has a special place in worship and supplies the public offerings, but he is not a priest.

Weights and measures were a constant temptation in trade. Merchants weighed silver against stones, and a heavier stone for buying and a lighter one for selling was an easy way to cheat. The law and the prophets condemn it again and again.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You shall maintain honest scales and weights’ (Leviticus 19:36). Proverbs says, ‘Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD’ (Proverbs 11:1).
passages.asks: God's vision of a holy people includes honest scales. Ask where you might be cutting corners at work or in money. And ask what it would mean for your dealings to reflect God's holiness.

passages.happening:
The people are to give the prince a modest share of their grain, oil and flock for the offerings (verses 13-16). ‘And it shall be the prince’s part to provide the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings for the feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths’ (verse 17), to make atonement for the house of Israel.

On the first day of the first month a young bull is to be offered to cleanse the sanctuary, and again on the seventh day for anyone who has sinned in error (verses 18-20). ‘On the fourteenth day of the first month you are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days, during which unleavened bread shall be eaten’ (verse 21). In the seventh month there is to be a feast of seven days with the same offerings (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The contributions are modest and proportional: a sixtieth of grain, a hundredth of oil, one sheep in two hundred. The prince is responsible for the public offerings, a reversal of kings who took from the people.

The calendar differs from the law of Moses in notable ways. It opens with purification rites in the first month that have no exact parallel there, counts the animals differently, and does not mention the Feast of Weeks or the Day of Atonement.
passages.later: The law set Passover ‘at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month’ (Leviticus 23:5). Amos condemned those eager to ‘cheat with dishonest scales’ (Amos 8:5).
passages.hard:
Why does Ezekiel's worship calendar differ from the law of Moses?

The differences are real, and interpreters explain them in several ways; this site takes no side. Some see Ezekiel giving a new, idealized law for the restored community, not meant to repeal Moses but to express the holiness of a new age in fresh terms. Others think Ezekiel records priestly practice of his own time, which varied from the written law. Those who expect a literal future temple often argue that the changes suit a different era of God's dealings with Israel, though the text itself uses the word atonement. Many Christian interpreters read the vision as symbolic, so that the changed details signal that the old order is not simply being restored. Jewish tradition felt the difficulty keenly and resolved it by harmonizing the texts.

The shared point is that worship in the restored community would be ordered, generous and centered on God's holiness.
passages.asks: The prince was to give for the people's worship instead of taking from them. Ask whether your use of power or money gives or takes. And ask what generosity toward God's people would look like for you.
